newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ report recommends lowering drinking age to 18.
newsitem.headline: NZ report recommends lowering drinking age to 18.

text.p: A government advisory committee on Tuesday recommended New Zealand drop its minimum age for buying alcohol to 18 from 20.
It also said restrictions on Sunday and supermarket sales should be relaxed.
Under current rules off-licences and supermarkets cannot sell any liquor on Sundays and supermarkets are only allowed to sell table wine on the other days of the week.
The committee said restrictions on Sunday trading were inconsistent and almost unenforceable. It saw it as no longer appropriate to restrict Sunday sales on religious grounds.
Justice Minister Doug Graham on Tuesday said the committee believed its recommendations should be accepted as a package.
"The advisory committee believes significant changes may well upset the balance of the package and detract from the value of the review they have undertaken," Graham said.
He said other government departments would now be asked to comment on the recommendations.
Any changes to the law are likely to be the subject of a free, or conscience vote, in parliament making the outcome difficult to predict.
The committee recommended dropping the age limit on drinking to 18 and said those younger than 18 should be able to be on licenced premises and drink if they are accompanied by a parent or guardian.
In a review of rules last overhauled in 1989 it also advocated retaining existing drinking hours and removing trading privileges for regional Licensing Trusts.
It rejected as impracticable the introduction of a national identity card for buying alcohol.
The report made no recommendations on health warnings pending the outcome of a report by the Australian and New Zealand Food Authority.
New Zealand's total alcohol consumption has fallen 22 percent since 1978 and in the main centres a noticeable cafe culture is developing as attitudes to drink move closer to those of Europe.
Across the country there has been a sharp reduction in sales of beer and spirits, while wine consumption rose 11 percent between 1986 and 1994.
